I am now calculating the cost of building a light blue monopoly. Unmortgaging both properties would cost about $121, leaving roughly $242 to build four houses at $50 each. That would leave only $42, so the opponent could not fully develop the set.

A light blue monopoly would be lethal. Connecticut and Vermont hotels could rent $550 to $600, threatening my $535 cash. A pink monopoly is also dangerous. St Charles and States together cost about $154 to unmortgage, leaving roughly $209 for two houses that would rent $300 to $360. No trade is worth it.

I need to make a Monopoly decision.

Only p4 remains. I'm on STATES_AVENUE with $535. My light blues and pinks are mortgaged and incomplete. I'm checking which orange properties I own.

I own all three orange properties: St. James, Tennessee, and New York. They are mortgaged but form a complete monopoly.

I have all three red properties with houses: Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois. I own Ventnor mortgaged and Pennsylvania mortgaged. Both hotels are on Park Place and Boardwalk. p4 has the brown monopoly with hotels and holds both utilities.

p4 owns St. Charles mortgaged, Virginia unmortgaged, Oriental, Marvin Gardens, Pacific, and North Carolina unmortgaged. They also hold GOOJF cards and both utilities.

I am recalculating p4's liquidation value. Boardwalk hotel rent is $2000 and Park Place hotel rent is $1500. Brown hotels sell for half their building cost.

Selling a hotel returns half its cost, which equals one house. This yields four houses that can be sold for half price each.

p4's cash has dropped to $363. Their prior liquidation estimate was roughly $1733, which could cover the $1700 four-house Boardwalk rent but not the $2000 hotel rent. I need to verify whether this lower cash balance still allows them to survive the hotel rent.

I am summing the mortgage values of p4's remaining unmortgaged properties. The total is $980.

p4's total liquidation is $1593. This is below the $2000 Boardwalk hotel rent, so they would go bankrupt there. It exceeds the $1500 Park Place hotel rent, meaning they could survive that but would have only about $93 left over. I am now questioning whether mortgaging properties that already have hotels is calculated correctly.

The $250 building sale is confirmed as half the total hotel cost. I am now determining whether this turn is my post-roll action phase or if I have already rolled.

I am in the post-turn action phase. I own States but it is mortgaged so I collect no rent there. I am deciding between building more houses on the red properties or taking another action.

Building one more house on Kentucky would raise its rent to $250. That is not enough to kill p4, since their liquidation value is only about $1593.

Three houses on the red properties would still not kill p4. A hotel on Illinois would only yield $1100 in rent.

Unmortgaging all three orange properties costs about $308. That leaves roughly $227 for two houses. That is too little to threaten p4 quickly.

I am weighing whether to spend cash on unmortgaging or building. I can afford the brown hotel rent of $450, leaving $85, and the Mediterranean hotel rent of $250. Unmortgaging all three oranges would drain my cash too much.

I also notice that p4's pink monopoly is incomplete because St. Charles is mortgaged. Virginia alone cannot collect rent while that property is mortgaged.

I now see that p4 has no active monopolies. Their only threatening rent is the $450 Baltic hotel. I can afford both brown hotels, but spending below $450 would leave me bankrupt on Baltic. I am now considering a trade.

I have decided against trading. I will not give away Pennsylvania or cash, since neither helps me win and both could strengthen p4. I also see no benefit in acquiring their brown properties. The best move is to end the turn. I will keep my cash above $450 to stay safe from the Baltic hotel rent. Unmortgaging anything would waste money without creating a faster kill than the Boardwalk hotel already provides.

Building another house on Kentucky would leave only $385, which is below the $450 Baltic hotel rent. That would bankrupt me if I land there. Selling buildings would also weaken the kill, so I will not do that either. I am now considering whether any trade could steal their cash or GOOJF cards without giving them a monopoly.

message.reasoning:
I'm ready to play Monopoly and make a decision.

I'm player 2 with $520 cash and a full set of mortgaged light blues and pinks. I just paid $90 rent to the last opponent, GPT-6.1-Sol. My reds are heavily invested with one house on Indiana and two on Illinois. The B&O railroad is also mortgaged.

I also own two hotels on dark blues. The last opponent has $453 cash and is in jail with a Get Out of Jail Free card. They have hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic, plus partial yellows and pinks.

The Boardwalk hotel is worth $2000, which would bankrupt the opponent if their liquidation is roughly $1683. The Park Place hotel is only $1500, so it would not finish them off. I will keep Illinois at two houses to drain cash while maintaining even building across the reds.

I realized my reds are uneven: one house on Indiana and two on Illinois. I should build on Kentucky and Indiana to match. I am now calculating the opponent's liquidation value.

I am calculating the opponent's liquidation value by selling their hotels for half their purchase price. I am also recalling standard house prices by color to determine how much cash they would have if forced to sell all buildings.

I am now calculating the exact cash value of each opponent's hotel if forced to sell. A Mediterranean hotel sells for $25, which reverts it to four houses worth $100 total. The bank still has 28 houses and 8 hotels available.

Baltic hotel also sells for $125, so the opponent's buildings total $250. I am now listing mortgage values for their remaining unmortgaged properties to complete the liquidation estimate.

The opponent's liquidation totals $1683. Boardwalk hotel rent is $2000, so they cannot pay and will go bankrupt. Park Place hotel rent is only $1500, which they can afford with leftover cash. The kill shot must be Boardwalk.

The opponent may stay in jail to avoid Boardwalk. I cannot force them onto that space. I will not trade them cash or properties that would help them survive the $2000 hotel rent.

Building on Kentucky and Indiana would cost $300, leaving me with $220 cash. I am now calculating the rent values for red properties once they are fully upgraded.

I confirmed the official rent schedule for red properties. Indiana and Kentucky each cost $90 per house. Illinois costs $100 per house. Two houses on Illinois equals $300 in rent.

Building more reds would not finish the opponent off. An Illinois hotel still leaves them with roughly $570 in liquidation, which is survivable. I also need to keep cash on hand to pay their brown hotels if I land there. A single house costs $150 and would leave me with only $370, which is too little to cover a Baltic hotel hit of $450 without selling buildings first.

Selling the Boardwalk hotel would drop its rent from $2000 to $1700. That is still $17 short of the opponent's liquidation of $1683, so it would barely finish them off. If I must sell that hotel to pay rent, I lose the kill shot. Landing on Baltic with only $520 leaves me with just $70 cash.

I will keep the Boardwalk hotel intact. If I must sell it to pay rent, the rent drops to $1700 and I may need to sell more houses to survive. Rent from utilities and railroads is manageable. The only dangerous squares are the brown hotels.

I need to keep $450 cash to survive a Baltic hotel hit without selling the Boardwalk hotel. I will not spend any money this turn. Unmortgaging properties would cost extra interest and is not worth it. I am checking which color sets are complete.

I do not own complete color sets among my mortgaged properties. Unmortgaging would only yield modest rent, so it is not worth the cost.

I considered trading my mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue to the opponent. That would complete their green color set and give them a major income boost. I rejected this because it would help them survive the Boardwalk hotel rent.

I considered trading my mortgaged Ventnor Avenue, but the opponent still needs Atlantic to complete a yellow monopoly. That would not finish me off immediately, though it is still undesirable.

I am now looking for a trade that gives me cash without handing the opponent a dangerous color set. Their Get Out of Jail Free card is not useful to me, but taking it would force them to roll or pay $50 to leave jail eventually.

Taking the opponent's Get Out of Jail Free card would force them onto the board where they can land on Boardwalk. I rejected a cash-for-GOOJF offer because it would reduce my own cash buffer while giving them money to survive the hotel rent. I also realized that offering any mortgaged property in exchange would increase their liquidation value, since they could mortgage it.

I realized that giving the opponent a mortgaged property would not increase their liquidation value. They cannot mortgage it again for cash, so that trade would not help them survive the Boardwalk hotel rent.

Mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue would complete the opponent's green color set. They would unmortgage it for $176 and build houses, turning Pacific, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania Avenue into hotels that cost $1275 to $1400 each. That is far too dangerous to trade.

I confirmed that giving away mortgaged properties would not complete any color sets for the opponent. They already own Oriental, so neither Vermont nor Connecticut would finish a light blue set. Ventnor is also not worth trading since it cannot complete their yellow set.

I also considered trading both Vermont and Connecticut to the opponent. That would complete a light blue monopoly, though it would not instantly bankrupt me. I still refuse to give them any color set that could become dangerous.

I also checked whether giving away States Avenue would complete a pink monopoly for them. They already own Virginia and St Charles, so that trade would indeed finish their pink set.

I confirmed that giving away States Avenue would complete the opponent's pink color set. Orange properties and railroads are also not worth trading, since they do not finish a set and would only slightly increase their rent. I am now considering whether to ask the opponent for cash or their Get Out of Jail Free card in exchange for nothing.

I rejected the idea of proposing a deceptive trade. The opponent is smart and would reject bad offers, so I will not waste a turn action on a proposal that could backfire.

I am now calculating how much cash I need to take from the opponent. Their liquidation is $1683, which is $317 short of the $2000 Boardwalk hotel rent. If they pass GO and collect $200, their liquidation rises to $1883, leaving only a $117 gap. Any extra cash would shrink that margin further.

I realized that if the opponent lands on Baltic before hitting Boardwalk, they gain $450 and their liquidation becomes $2133. That is enough to survive the $2000 hotel rent with $133 left over. The order of landings matters. I cannot control dice to avoid landing on Baltic. I am now looking for a way to force them to spend cash so that even a Baltic rent would not save them.

I calculated that the opponent must be liquidated below $1350 to survive a Baltic rent plus passing GO. Currently their liquidation is $1683, so I need to extract roughly $333 or destroy their assets. I cannot destroy their properties directly; only rent payments can reduce them. If they land on my properties before I land on Baltic, they pay rent and are nearly bankrupt.

Building three houses on Illinois Avenue would raise rent to $750, but it costs $150 in construction and leaves only $370 cash. That is still too little to cover a Baltic hotel hit of $450 without selling more buildings. This exposes the core cash management problem.

I will not build houses this turn. The minimum construction cost is $150, leaving only $370 cash after building. That is still $80 short of the $450 Baltic hotel rent. Selling one Illinois house for $75 would leave me $5 short. I cannot sell more houses from Illinois without violating the rule that requires keeping at least as many houses on Illinois as on Kentucky or Indiana.

I can sell one house from each of the three red properties, since they are all at one house. That would raise cash by $225, but it would also reduce rent on those properties. It still does not force the opponent to sell their Boardwalk hotel.

Building one house is not worth the cost, since the rent increase would not kill them and I would still need to sell more buildings to cover a Baltic hotel hit. I will not unmortgage properties either, because that costs money and does not complete a color set. I am now considering whether to propose a deceptive trade that offers the opponent something they want in exchange for cash, though I expect them to reject it.

I am now considering a trade that would buy the opponent's brown hotels. That would eliminate the $450 and $250 rent threat from Mediterranean and Baltic, but paying cash for those properties would give them money to survive the Boardwalk hotel.

I calculated that buying both brown hotels would cost roughly $200, netting the opponent a $110 loss while leaving them still bankrupt to Boardwalk. They would never accept such an offer. I am now looking for a trade that gives them a viable path to survive or kill me.

I considered trading mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue to the opponent for cash. That would give them a green monopoly and extra cash, but it would also let them build hotels costing over $1400 each. I rejected this trade because it is too dangerous.

I will end my turn. I will not trade away any color set that could become dangerous, including green, pink, or light blue properties. I will keep my public message brief and avoid revealing strategy.

I confirmed the opponent's liquidation is $1683. Boardwalk hotel at $2000 leaves a $317 gap, while four houses on Baltic at $1700 leaves only a $17 gap. I have a $70 cushion against the $450 Baltic hotel rent. The opponent is in jail with a Get Out of Jail Free card and may stay there to avoid the board. I cannot force them out without giving them more resources. I am now considering whether to attempt one last probe trade for their card.

I considered offering a mortgaged railroad for the opponent's Get Out of Jail Free card. That trade would not add liquidation, and the rent from one mortgaged railroad is only $50 until unmortgaged. The opponent would reject it because jail safety is worth more than the mortgage cost.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

### Strategy Guidance

- Observe opponents and adapt.

- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

message.reasoning:
I am reviewing the Monopoly game state to determine my next move.

Only one opponent remains. I have $245 and am at COMMUNITY_CHEST. My dark blue hotels are my win condition. I recently built houses on the reds. Most of my other properties are mortgaged. The remaining opponent has $1003 and owns Mediterranean and Baltic with hotels.

The opponent's liquid assets total $2233. Boardwalk costs $2000, so I need to drain them by at least $234 to win. I will hit the reds before any hotels and before passing GO. The reds cost $300 and leave me with $245, which is enough. Baltic is after GO, so I will sell one house on Illinois to cover the gap. I will not unmortgage St Charles or trade away Pennsylvania, States, or Vermont and Connecticut. I will end my turn next.

The opponent cannot land on my reds this turn. A roll of 2-12 from Vermont Avenue only reaches Jail through Free Parking, which is before the reds begin at space 21. I will wait for a future turn to hit those properties.

Boardwalk is not an immediate threat. The opponent can still pay the $2000 rent from liquid assets alone. A single red hit of $250 leaves them with $1983, which is still below the $2000 mark. I must drain them by at least $234 before they can land on Boardwalk.

A single red landing is enough to make Boardwalk lethal. I have $245, so I can build one more house on Illinois for $150 and raise rent to $750, leaving me with $95. I am weighing whether the Baltic Avenue cushion is worth keeping.

I am determining which of the three Community Chest spaces I occupy. A roll from space 17 would land on my own properties. A roll from space 33 would reach Park Place or Boardwalk.

I am on Community Chest space 17. A roll of 2-12 lands on my mortgaged properties, unowned Atlantic Avenue, and their utilities Water Works and Marvin Gardens.

The utilities and Marvin Gardens are all affordable. I will not go bankrupt from the next roll. I cannot land on Baltic from this position.

The Baltic Avenue hotel costs $450. After passing GO, I would have $445 and be short by $5. I will sell one house on Illinois for $75 to cover the gap. The Kentucky and Indiana properties will stay at two houses each.

I will keep all three red properties at two houses. Selling one house now would only raise rent to $100, which is too little to drain enough cash. I will only sell an Illinois house if forced to pay the Baltic hotel after passing GO. The utilities and Marvin Gardens are affordable from this position. A bad Chance card could still hit me before reaching GO.

A "general repairs" Chance card would cost $350. That exceeds my $245 cash and would force me to sell buildings.

I will not build more houses on the reds. The extra rent is unnecessary and would leave me more vulnerable to repairs. I will also avoid unmortgaging properties, since the cost is too high.

Unmortgaging Pennsylvania would cost $176, but the opponent already owns the other greens and would not gain a monopoly. I will not trade away mortgaged properties to them.

I will never trade away mortgaged properties to the opponent. Completing their light blue group with Vermont and Connecticut would let them build hotels and kill me. Completing their green group with Pennsylvania Avenue would do the same. I will keep my full red monopoly intact.

I am considering proposing a trade for cash. The opponent has $1003 and may not overpay for mortgaged railroads or other properties. If they reject, I will continue without building.

I am weighing whether to propose a trade now. A single red hit leaves the opponent with $1983, still above the $1500 threshold for Park Place. Two hits leave them at $1683, also above that mark. Only three hits or a hotel-level rent would drain enough cash to make Park Place lethal. Boardwalk only needs $234, so one two-house red hit is sufficient.

Building three houses on all reds would cost $450, which exceeds my available cash of $245. Even one additional house on Illinois would raise rent to $750, leaving the opponent with only $1483 after paying that rent from their liquid assets.

I will not build a third house on Illinois. The $150 cost leaves only $95, which is too risky if I hit Water Works before I can sell it back. Even if I must sell a house to pay a debt, I can return Illinois to two houses without breaking the even-building rule.

I am calculating the exact distances from my current position. The reds are 13, 15, and 16 spaces away, while GO is 32. This means the opponent would pass GO before reaching any red property.

The opponent will land on a red property before passing GO. From their current position, a second roll of 2-12 can reach the reds at spaces 21, 23, and 24. They may also land on utilities or other properties in that same turn.

The opponent cannot land on Park Place or Boardwalk this turn. They can reach the reds next turn, but not the hotels until the following turn. If they hit a red and drain enough cash, they will likely land on Boardwalk in the next turn and bankrupt. If they miss the reds, they may survive by landing on hotels with full liquid assets. Building more houses does not increase the probability of hitting those properties. Cash conservation is the correct strategy.

Unmortgaging any property would cost more than the rent collected. The opponent already owns Virginia and St Charles, so States cannot complete a monopoly. The base rent on every unmortgaged property is too low to justify the $77 to $110 unmortgage fees.

I considered selling railroads to the opponent for cash, but that would give them four railroads and raise my own rent to $200. That is too dangerous for me.

I own all three orange properties, but they are mortgaged and generate no rent. I could trade one orange for cash without giving the opponent a monopoly.

I cannot unmortgage all three orange properties with my current cash, so selling one would only sacrifice future building options. A rejected trade wastes a message and offers no clear benefit. I will only propose a trade if it is clearly favorable even if accepted.

A trade for a single mortgaged property would be rejected by a rational opponent, since it would cost them more to unmortgage than the rent they would collect. Offering both Vermont and Connecticut to complete their light blue set would also be unwise, as they already own hotels on those spaces.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.

- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I have $1295 and am on CONNECTICUT_AVENUE. Most of my properties are mortgaged. I own reds with four houses each and two mortgaged railroads.

I own two dark blues with hotels. The last opponent is on Oriental Avenue with only $223 cash and cannot reach my reds this turn. Their hotel rent would still exceed their liquid assets. I will build four houses on my reds now.

I will now build hotels on the reds. This costs $450 and leaves $845 cash, which covers the $450 rent for Baltic Avenue. I will not unmortgage or trade.

I realized that building hotels is necessary to guarantee a kill on any red property, not just Illinois. A 4-house hit on Kentucky or Indiana leaves only $8 cash after passing GO, which is enough to survive. However, a hotel hit on those properties would still eliminate them even after receiving GO money. I am now tracing the exact path from Oriental Avenue to determine which reds they might land on.

The opponent will reach the reds before passing GO. They need only 15 to 18 spaces from Oriental Avenue, which can be covered in two or three rolls. This means they will not collect $200 on their first lap around the board.

I am now weighing whether the opponent might skip the reds entirely. If they land on Free Parking or pass them, they would travel past my mortgaged greens and eventually reach my dark blue hotels at Park Place and Boardwalk. Those hotels cost $1500 and $2000, which would instantly eliminate them.

The opponent cannot skip the reds entirely. Those properties occupy four consecutive spaces, so they must land on at least one of them before passing GO.

The opponent can skip the reds entirely. From St. James Place, a roll of nine or higher jumps past all three red properties. From Tennessee Avenue, a roll of seven or higher skips them. From New York Avenue, a roll of six or higher bypasses them completely.

A roll of five or higher from Free Parking also bypasses the reds. After skipping them, the opponent would pass my mortgaged railroads and greens, then land on my dark blue hotels at Park Place and Boardwalk. Those hotels cost $1500 and $2000, which would instantly eliminate them.

I also considered that if the opponent skips the reds and dark blues, passes GO for $200, and lands on a non-lethal property, they could survive. But Chance and Community Chest cards could still provide enough cash to kill them later. Building hotels is the only way to guarantee the elimination.

I cannot land on Baltic Avenue next turn from Connecticut. I would need to travel 34 spaces around the board. The opponent's unmortgaged rent-charging properties are Mediterranean, Baltic, Electric Company, and Water Works. My next roll from Connecticut will reach spaces 10 through 21.

I can land on Electric Company next turn. Rent there is only $120, so building hotels now is safe and I should proceed immediately.

I will build hotels on all three red properties in a single action. The even-build rule allows this since each currently has four houses. I have no orange or pink monopolies to unmortgage.

I confirmed the opponent's total liquid assets are $683. Selling both brown hotels and four houses yields $250, plus mortgage values of $60 on Mediterranean and Baltic, and $150 on both utilities. This leaves them with only $683 to cover rent.

I checked whether a lucky Chance card could save the opponent. Even a $200 dividend plus GO money leaves only about $33 after paying a hotel on Kentucky Avenue. Illinois Avenue still kills them.

A $1000 hotel on Kentucky or Indiana leaves the opponent with only $33, so they survive. An $1100 hotel on Illinois kills them. The narrow survival scenario requires drawing a specific card, passing GO, landing on the right property, and mortgaging everything in time. Birthday or opera cards would add only $10. Building more than hotels is impossible, so the hotel strategy remains correct.

I considered unmortgaging cheap properties to drain the opponent before they reach the reds, but every space on their path from Oriental Avenue is mortgaged. Hotels remain the only viable strategy.

Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue for $99 would only charge $14 rent, which is negligible. Unmortgaging all three pinks costs $275 and would require building houses at $100 each. I am now checking the exact rent values for those properties to see if that path could be worthwhile.

Unmortgaging all three pinks and building houses would cost $1475, which exceeds my available cash of $1295. Even building three houses on each pink costs $1175, leaving only $120 afterward. That is not enough to kill the opponent and still cover the $450 rent for Baltic Avenue.

I ruled out building two houses on the reds because the rent would be too low and the cost too high. Unmortgaging the light blues still cannot complete a monopoly. I also rejected draining cash by unmortgaging properties they will land on, since the interest and reduced cash cushion outweigh any benefit. I briefly considered unmortgaging the B&O Railroad, but that would cost $110 and only yield $25 in rent, which is not worth it.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I have $1295 and am on PENNSYLVANIA_RAILROAD. Most of my properties are mortgaged, though the orange and dark blue monopolies are fully built. I need to decide whether to unmortgage, build, or trade.

The private thought about hotels on the reds was from turn 127. The current state shows four houses on each red property and $1295 cash. I am reconciling this discrepancy.

I will build hotels on the red properties. Each hotel costs $150, so three hotels total $450. This leaves me with $845 in cash.

Player four has $223 and owns hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic. I am calculating how much cash they could raise by selling those hotels back.

Selling a hotel returns half its purchase price and four houses. The bank has enough houses to cover this. Player four's full liquidation is roughly $683, including the two brown hotels at $250 each.

Selling a hotel returns $125 per property, or $250 total for both brown hotels. Unmortgaged utilities add $150, and mortgaged deeds add $60.

I am calculating the rent values for the red properties with four houses. Kentucky Avenue and Indiana Avenue each pay $875 per visit. Illinois Avenue pays $925.

Player four's liquid assets of roughly $683 cannot cover the $875 rent on any red property. Even with hotels, the rent would still exceed their cash. I am now checking the board order to see if player four can land on a red before passing GO.

I mapped the board positions. Player four on St. Charles Place can land on Electric Company, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, Pennsylvania Railroad, St. James Place, or the Community Chest.

Player four can land on Kentucky Avenue with an 11, which kills them. Indiana and Illinois are unreachable from St. Charles Place this turn. The next roll is from Pennsylvania Railroad.

Player four cannot land on my brown hotels this turn. Mediterranean is 26 spaces away and Baltic is 27. I am safe from rent this roll. I am now questioning why I should build hotels.

Player four's cash would rise to roughly $883 after passing GO. This would cover the $875 rent on Kentucky and Indiana Avenue, but not the $925 rent on Illinois Avenue. I am now checking whether they can liquidate their brown hotels instantly to pay rent.

Selling a hotel returns four houses to the bank. Those houses can then be sold for $25 each, yielding $100 per property. Player four's total liquidation is therefore roughly $683.

They could also mortgage their unmortgaged properties for an additional $210. This brings their total available cash to about $893.

Player four would survive the $875 rent on Kentucky and Indiana Avenue after passing GO, but still die on Illinois Avenue. Hotel rents of $1050 and $1100 would kill them even with a $200 chance card.

Hotels extend the kill window. Player four would survive the $1050 hotel rent on Kentucky and Indiana Avenue after two GO laps, but still die to the $1100 hotel rent on Illinois Avenue.

Building hotels is a clear upgrade. Four houses on the reds only survive one GO lap, but hotels kill all three reds immediately. I will have $845 left after the $450 investment. That covers the $450 rent on the Baltic hotel and leaves $395. The Mediterranean hotel costs $250. Taxes are manageable.

Monopoly rules allow hotels to count as five houses, so building all three reds at once keeps the properties evenly matched. Partial hotels would leave some properties vulnerable after one GO lap, so I will build all three.

I am checking whether to unmortgage New York Avenue. It is the only mortgaged orange property, costing $110 to unmortgage. I am also verifying the standard color group assignments to confirm which properties belong to each monopoly.

I now see that my pink monopoly is incomplete. I own States Avenue but not St. Charles Place, which player four holds mortgaged. I also own St. James Place and Tennessee Avenue as orange properties, not pink. This means I do not fully control the pink color group.

I own all three orange properties, but they are all mortgaged. Unmortgaging the entire orange monopoly would cost $308. Once built, orange houses would generate rent of $14, $70, $200, $550, $750, and $950 per visit.

I cannot build hotels on the orange properties. The total cost is $1808, but I only have $1295. Three houses would cost $1208 and leave me with just $87, which is too little to cover the Baltic hotel rent.

I will not unmortgage the orange properties now. The red hotels remain the priority.

Trading with player four is unwise. They already hold brown hotels that hurt me, and they have almost no cash. I should avoid giving them anything that would help them survive or raise their funds.

I am now considering whether to sell any buildings.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I am now checking whether the opponent can draw a $200 chance card and pass GO before landing on a red property. From St. Charles Place, they must travel 29 spaces to reach GO, which normally requires at least three turns unless they draw an "advance to GO" card. The relevant chance cards are "advance to GO," "bank pays $50," and "advance to Illinois."

The opponent can land on a Chance space at 22, eleven spaces from St. Charles Place. That card could send them to Boardwalk, which would kill me instantly with its $2000 hotel rent. It could also send them to Illinois or Reading, or let them pass GO for $200.

Four houses on Kentucky and Indiana would barely survive a pass through GO, leaving only about eight dollars in cash. Hotels guarantee a kill in every scenario, so I will build all three now. I am now mapping the opponent's remaining squares from St. Charles Place. The utilities are not a concern because the dice are already known. I noted that Atlantic Avenue is unowned and could be bought, but the green monopoly is incomplete. I also verified that the opponent's mortgaged properties cannot charge rent, and I am checking whether the Luxury Tax is $75 or $100.

I confirmed that passing GO before landing on the reds is safe, since cash would reach roughly $1045. I am now drafting the build plan to place hotels on Kentucky Avenue and Indiana Avenue.

The build plan is finalized. Hotels will be placed on all three red properties. The bank has eight hotels and twenty houses available, so there are no supply constraints. All three spaces already have four houses, making the upgrade evenly balanced. I will now execute the construction.

message.reasoning:
The user is playing Monopoly as player p2.

Evaluating p4's trade counter. I would give $900 cash for PACIFIC_AVENUE and NORTH_CAROLINA_AVENUE, both mortgaged. I own PENNSYLVANIA_AVENUE mortgaged.

Marvin Gardens remains with p4. I would own Pacific, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania Avenue, but that does not complete the green set.

Accepting the trade would complete the green monopoly. The total unmortgage cost is $506, which exceeds my remaining cash of $175 after paying $900.

I cannot unmortgage the three greens immediately. p4 has hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic, which would cost $250 and $450 in rent. My red and dark-blue hotels already kill p4 even after full liquidation. After accepting the trade, p4 would have roughly $1393 cash plus remaining assets.

Mortgaged properties likely contribute little to liquidation value. Pacific and North Carolina would not add much cash if p4 were forced to sell.

Selling p4's brown hotels would return $250. Unmortgaged utilities are worth $75 each.

p4's liquidation value is roughly $953. After receiving $900, it rises to about $1853. Red hotel rents alone would no longer guarantee a bankruptcy. Park Place at $1500 would still kill them, leaving only $353 remaining.

Boardwalk at $2000 would still kill p4, but red hotel rents would not. I cannot afford to accept the trade because $175 cash is too low to cover a $450 Baltic hotel rent. Selling my red and dark-blue hotels for liquidity is possible but disastrous. I am now considering a counter-offer.

I am checking whether p4 already owns complete color sets. They have all three pink properties mortgaged, but States Avenue belongs to me. I own Vermont and Connecticut mortgaged, while they hold Oriental mortgaged. This leaves the light blue set incomplete.

I own all three orange properties mortgaged. I hold Ventnor in yellow while p4 owns Marvin Gardens; Atlantic is unowned, so no one can monopolize yellow. Both my and p4's railroads are mortgaged. The $900 trade for two mortgaged greens is a clear bad deal.

I will reject the trade. I cannot afford to unmortgage and build on the greens, and giving p4 cash would reduce my kill power. My existing hotels already guarantee their bankruptcy. The original offer of Pennsylvania Avenue for $400 would have completed their green monopoly.
